metrics.label: Bot share of supply
metrics.definition: Tokens bought by bots at launch ÷ all tokens bought at launch.

metrics.label: Bot profit
metrics.definition: USDC bots receive selling to later human buyers, minus what they paid for the tokens they sold. Tokens they cannot sell count as zero.

metrics.label: Human price premium
metrics.definition: Median price per token paid by humans who got tokens (launch plus pool) ÷ the average price bots paid at launch.

metrics.label: Humans filled
metrics.definition: Share of the humans holding any tokens at the end, from the launch or the pool.

metrics.label: Holder concentration
metrics.definition: Gini coefficient of final holdings across every account holding tokens. 0 = equal, 1 = one holder.

assumptions: Supply for sale: 1,000,000 tokens. Reference launch price: 0.01 USDC per token, so selling the whole supply at that price raises 10,000 USDC.
Demand level = total human budget ÷ (supply × launch price). 60 runs, evenly spaced from 0.5x to 4x. Each run draws a fresh crowd from its own seed, derived from base seed 20261114.
200 humans per run. Each has a private valuation, the most they would pay per token: lognormal, median 1.6x the launch price, sigma 0.55, clamped to 0.3x–12x. Valuations are never shown.
Human budgets are lognormal weights (sigma 0.9, so a few whales) scaled to the demand level, at least 1 USDC each. Humans arrive between second 1 and second 1,800, more of them early.

5 sniper bots per run, each with a budget of 2%–6% of the supply value (200–600 USDC). Bots act at second 0, before any human. On the bonding curve and in the fixed-price sale they buy with their whole budget. In Sealround they bid their whole budget with a max price of 100x the launch price.

Bonding curve: constant product x·y = k with virtual reserves in pump.fun proportions (virtual token reserve = 1.3529 × the curve supply). The virtual USDC reserve is set so buying the whole curve raises 10,000 USDC, the same as the fixed-price sale. The price runs from 0.002608 to 0.038335 USDC (0.26x to 3.83x the launch price).

On the curve, buyers act in arrival order. A human buys until their budget runs out or the price reaches their valuation. The curve is a two-way market from second 0, so after each human buy, bots sell back into it with the same rule as the post-launch pool (below). The launch ends when the curve sells out or the last human has arrived.
Fixed-price sale: 0.01 USDC per token, first come first served until supply runs out. A human buys only if their valuation is at least the price.

Sealround: every human whose valuation is at or above the floor (the launch price) bids max price = valuation and max spend = deposit = whole budget. Humans below the floor do not bid. Clearing uses clear() from @fairground/clearing, the same rule the enclave runs. Unsold tokens are burned.
Humans are honest and simple: they bid their true valuation in Sealround and stop at it on the curve. Nobody splits across wallets.

Post-launch market, identical for all three: a constant-product pool opens at the launch's final price (curve: its last price; fixed price: 0.01; Sealround: the clearing price) with 2,000 USDC of liquidity (20% of the supply value) paired with tokens at that price.
Humans with budget left and a valuation above the pool price buy from the pool in arrival order, each until their budget runs out or the price reaches their valuation.

Bots sell into that demand: after each human buy, bots sell back until the price returns to where it was before that buy. A bot never sells below what it paid per token. Tokens bots cannot sell stay in their wallets.

Bot profit counts only tokens actually sold, at the average price the bot paid. Unsold tokens count as zero, not at a market value. Bots follow this one simple selling rule everywhere; bots that time their sales better would likely make more on the curve and in the fixed-price sale, so those profits are conservative.
No fees, gas, latency or MEV beyond bots acting first. Money is integer throughout (USDC 6 decimals, tokens 18 decimals); floats appear only in the reported metrics.
Deterministic: the same seed and config give byte-identical output. No LLM calls, no network.
